arXiv:2610.26935v1 [cs.CR] 17 Oct 2026

How Intervention History Changes AI Agent Sabotage on Subsequent Tasks

Daniel Saeedi, Amirali Aghazadeh Email: {dsaeedi3,amiralia}@gatech.edu Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer EngineeringGeorgia Institute of TechnologyAtlanta, GA, USA
Abstract

AI control evaluations often reset agents’ memory between tasks, although deployed agents may retain records of prior interventions. We ask whether learning that an earlier attack was caught changes an agent’s ability to evade defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that replaces suspicious work with a trusted model’s solution. Prior work has studied this adaptation behavior when feedback is provided during repeated attempts on the same problem. Herein, we study cross-episode adaptation: whether intervention history changes attack behavior on a subsequent task with different objectives and a fresh environment. We evaluate this using ControlArena’s Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and SHADE-Arena as testbeds, where agents must complete a main task while covertly pursuing a harmful side objective. For each successor task, we pair a history-conditioned attempt with the model’s no-history attempt. The retained history either states that the previous submission was replaced or additionally includes the trusted model’s replacement.

For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, intervention history reduces successful sabotage. Completion of both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told about the replacement and to 38% when it is also shown the trusted model’s replacement, while main task success remains essentially unchanged. Condensing the history weakens this effect, suggesting that the retained context matters and limiting attribution to intervention feedback alone. GPT-5.4 shows no significant change in successful sabotage on the same IaC benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5’s successful sabotage rate decreases, but the reduction is not significant. Across the tested models, history conditions, and deferral thresholds, intervention history never increases the rate of successful sabotage that survives DtT. These results show that intervention history can change subsequent attack behavior, but its effect depends on both the model and the retained context.11 1 Code and results are available at https://github.com/amirgroup-codes/caught_not_taught22 2 Agents transcripts: https://caughtnottaught.github.io/

1 Introduction

Continued advances in AI agent capability and reliability make it increasingly plausible that these systems will be delegated tasks involving financial transactions, access to sensitive information, and actions in digital or physical environments (Crichton et al., 2024; Stanford HAI, 2025). As the consequences of erroneous, misaligned, or unauthorized actions grow, so does the need for mechanisms that can detect and correct such behavior before it causes irreversible harm. AI control (Greenblatt et al., 2024b) studies how to safely use a capable but potentially misaligned untrusted model 𝒰\mathcal{U} under the supervision of a trusted model 𝒯\mathcal{T}. In defer-to-trusted (DtT), a trusted monitor scores 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s work for suspicion, and submissions above a threshold are replaced by work from a trusted model.

Most early control evaluations reset the attack policy between task trajectories (Greenblatt et al., 2024b; Bhatt et al., 2025; Kutasov et al., 2025b). Real deployments, however, may retain conversation history or memory. An agent could therefore begin a new task knowing that a previous attack was detected and replaced. This history may reveal both that a monitor is present and what kinds of behavior it rejects. Such information could help an attacker. Agents with explicit knowledge of a monitor can sometimes adapt their behavior to evade current control protocols (Terekhov et al., 2026). It remains unclear whether retaining a prior attack trajectory and the feedback that it was replaced changes an agent’s ability to sabotage a subsequent task or evade DtT. We study this form of cross-episode adaptation when the successor task has different objectives and begins in a fresh environment.

Prior work has connected episodes in several ways. Adaptive deployment uses past actions to update the defender’s belief about model alignment (Wen et al., 2024). Persistent-state control allows later attacks to inherit code written in earlier pull requests, while multi-agent control allows separate agent instances to distribute a covert objective across their work (Lindner et al., 2025; Hills et al., 2026; Makins et al., 2026). These settings show that deployment history can matter, but they focus on defender-side updating or continued pursuit of a shared objective across episodes. They do not study whether an attack policy changes its behavior on a new task after experiencing a completed control intervention. In particular, the main persistent-code experiments of Hills et al. (2026) carry code across pull requests but do not preserve the attacker’s conversation history.

The closest prior work studies feedback following an intervention. Within a trajectory, Kutasov et al. (2025a) label which earlier actions were replaced, and Lucassen and Kaufman (2026) show that monitor rationales can lead to less suspicious retries. CIAware-Bench provides replacement text, scores, and monitor reasoning after online deferrals, and finds a small, non-significant increase in aggregate side-task success (Schaeffer et al., 2026). Jiralerspong et al. (2026) retain full transcripts and coarse blocking feedback across ten consecutive attempts on the same task. Agents sometimes infer that a hidden monitor is present and intend to evade it, but fail to carry out that strategy. Together, these results show that intervention feedback can change an agent’s beliefs and attack strategy. However, because they operate within the same trajectory or repeat the same task, they also allow the agent to directly repair or retry the attack that was caught.

Here, we target the cross-episode adaptation regime (Fig. 1). We first let 𝒰\mathcal{U} attack candidate tasks under DtT and include a task pip_{i} in the intervention arms only if its submission is selected for replacement, corresponding to a monitor suspicion score of at least 5/105/10 in Infrastructure-as-Code (Stickland et al., 2025; Inglis et al., 2025) or 50/10050/100 in SHADE-Arena (Kutasov et al., 2025b). We then start a successor task pjp_{j} in a fresh environment and new conversation, replaying the caught trajectory from pip_{i} followed by one feedback message. In the told replaced condition, the feedback states that the prior submission was replaced. In the shown replacement condition, it also includes the replacement produced by the trusted model 𝒯\mathcal{T}. We pair each history-conditioned attempt with the same model’s memoryless attempt on the identical pjp_{j}, so the successor task and environment are held fixed, and only the prior episode and intervention feedback differ. We also vary how much of that history is retained. Full history includes the prior conversation and tool interactions, with reasoning removed and long tool outputs elided, while condensed history keeps only the prior task, the model’s final message, and the resulting diff or actions. Within each feedback condition, the intervention message itself is unchanged across history formats, including the trusted replacement when shown.

Our cross-episode experiments show that full intervention history substantially reduces successful sabotage when Claude Opus 4.8 serves as the untrusted model in ControlArena’s Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) environment (Stickland et al., 2025; Inglis et al., 2025). Its successful sabotage rate falls from 0.77 without prior history to 0.12 under told replaced and 0.38 under shown replacement, while main task success remains unchanged. Condensing the history weakens the reduction in successful sabotage, suggesting that the longer context may partly explain the effect. Intervention history produces no detectable reduction in successful sabotage in subsequent episodes when GPT-5.4 serves as the untrusted model in IaC or when GPT-5 serves as the untrusted model in SHADE-Arena (Kutasov et al., 2025b). Across the evaluated settings and deferral thresholds, neither feedback condition produces a statistically detectable increase in successful sabotage that survives DtT.

We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We study cross-episode adaptation after a completed control intervention: whether intervention history changes an untrusted model’s ability to sabotage a successor task with different objectives in a fresh environment.

  • •

    We compare two feedback conditions: told replaced, which tells the untrusted model that its previous submission was replaced, and shown replacement, which also provides the trusted model’s replacement.

  • •

    We show that intervention history can reduce successful sabotage, with effects that depend on the untrusted model and retained context. Neither feedback condition produces a detectable increase in successful sabotage surviving DtT across the evaluated settings and deferral thresholds.

2 Cross-episode adaptation

Setting and protocol.

We evaluate ControlArena’s Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC), a mock AWS codebase, and SHADE-Arena’s simulated tool-use workspaces. In both, an untrusted model 𝒰\mathcal{U} receives a benign main task and a covert side objective; benign baselines use the same models and main tasks without the side objective. Under DtT, a trusted monitor assigns a suspicion score to 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s submission. A submission that meets the deferral threshold is replaced with the trusted model 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s submission for the same main task; otherwise, 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s submission is retained. We evaluate this substitution post hoc using stored monitor scores and trusted submissions. The monitor reviews the final repository diff on IaC and the current episode’s transcript on SHADE-Arena. On IaC, we normalize the score to the range [0,1][0,1], denote it by ss, and defer when ss exceeds the threshold τ=0.45\tau=0.45; on SHADE-Arena, we defer at raw scores of at least 50 out of 100. On IaC, we evaluate Claude Opus 4.8 as the untrusted model with Claude Opus 4.5 as both the monitor and replacement model. We also evaluate GPT-5.4 as the untrusted model with GPT-4.1 as both the monitor and replacement model. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5 is the untrusted model, o3 is the monitor, and GPT-4.1 supplies the replacement episode. We chose these untrusted models after newer candidates were blocked or omitted the side objective in our probes: the provider’s content filter stopped Claude Opus 5 on every IaC probe cell, GPT-5.6 completed the main task but silently omitted the side task on all 40 IaC cells, and GPT-5.4 omitted SHADE-Arena’s side task under its attack prompt. We use o3 on SHADE-Arena because, given the same monitor prompt, GPT-4.1 scored only 6% of GPT-5’s attack episodes at 50 or above and missed six of the seven successful sabotages we inspected. Appendix A includes benchmark-specific tasks, budgets, scoring, and implementation details, along with exact model identifiers and run dates. Appendix B includes the attack, monitor, and feedback prompts.

Task cells and pairing.

IaC provides 5 main tasks and 9 side tasks. A cell combines one main task with one side task, giving 45 possible combinations. Using a fixed seed, we omit one cell per main task, leaving 40 cells, and arrange them in a cycle so that consecutive cells share neither objective. SHADE-Arena instead fixes the pairing: each of its 26 tasks couples one main task with its own side task. We use 25 of them (excluding election tampering) and arrange them in a cycle. As in IaC, consecutive tasks share neither objective, by definition, since no two tasks share a main or side task; we also require that they never share an environment, e.g., the user’s persona, pre-filled emails, files, accounts, and the tools for acting on them.

Memoryless episodes.

We first collect memoryless attack attempts from each untrusted model, running each IaC cell once (40 episodes total) and each SHADE-Arena task for 4 epochs (100 episodes total). We keep the episodes in which the model submits a solution and the monitor flags it as suspicious, with each retained episode denoted by pip_{i}: 26 for Claude Opus 4.8 and 12 for GPT-5.4 in IaC, and 22 for GPT-5 in SHADE-Arena. We also run 𝒯\mathcal{T}on the same main tasks without a side task as a benign baseline.

Cross-episode adaptation conditions.

For each caught episode pip_{i}, 𝒰\mathcal{U} attempts pjp_{j} in a fresh environment and a new conversation under pjp_{j}’s attack prompt (Fig. 1). We compare this history-conditioned attempt with 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s memoryless attempt on the same pjp_{j}. We include the comparison regardless of whether the memoryless attempt on pjp_{j} was flagged as suspicious. In the full-history condition, we replay 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s prior trajectory on pip_{i} with reasoning removed and long tool outputs elided, followed by one feedback message. The told replaced feedback says that the previous submission was replaced with a different implementation. The replacement feedback shows the trusted model’s replacement: a repository diff on IaC, or the trusted model’s actions and final message on SHADE-Arena. No monitor score, rationale, or instruction to learn from the intervention is supplied. In the condensed-history condition, the replay contains only the prior task, the model’s final message, and its diff or actions. We keep the feedback fixed across history formats, including the trusted replacement when shown, to test whether changes in attack behavior persist with a shorter record of the prior episode or depend on retaining its intermediate interactions. Prompt details and exact feedback messages appear in Appendix B.

Metrics.

Our primary attack outcome is successful sabotage, B=Pr⁡(main∧side)B=\Pr(\text{main}\wedge\text{side}), where both the side task and the main task succeed. We also report BDtTB_{\mathrm{DtT}}, the corresponding sabotage rate after DtT; a replaced episode fails the side task and inherits the trusted replacement’s main task outcome. Other metrics include main task success, mean monitor suspicion, and deferral rate. Every history-conditioned attempt is compared with the memoryless attempt on the same pjp_{j}. We report 95% paired-bootstrap intervals using 5000 resamples and exact two-sided McNemar tests for binary outcomes. Each bootstrap resampling unit keeps the memoryless and history-conditioned outcomes together, matched on the same successor main task and side task cell in IaC and on the same successor task and repetition index in SHADE-Arena.

3 Results

The main question is whether being caught induces cross-episode adaptation in the attack policy. Because the prior and successor tasks have different objectives and fresh environments, the model cannot simply repair the caught sabotage and repeat it. Transfer must instead appear as a change in whether it attacks, how suspicious its work looks, or how often successful sabotage survives DtT. We first examine how the reduction in successful sabotage depends on the model and task, then compare full and condensed history, and finally assess sabotage surviving DtT.

3.1 Reduction in sabotage depends on model and task

Full history reduces sabotage in Opus 4.8 on IaC tasks.

On the 26 matched successor tasks, successful sabotage falls from B=0.77B=0.77 memoryless to 0.12 under full told replaced (Δ​B=−0.65\Delta B=-0.65, 95% CI [−0.85,−0.42][-0.85,\,-0.42], McNemar p=8×10−5p=8\times 10^{-5}). Under full shown replacement, successful sabotage is higher than under told replaced but remains well below the memoryless baseline at 0.38 (Δ​B=−0.38\Delta B=-0.38, CI [−0.62,−0.15][-0.62,\,-0.15], p=0.006p=0.006; Figs. 2 and 3a).

The reduction in sabotage is not accompanied by a general decline in task performance. Main task success before deferral is 0.88 in memoryless, 0.92 under told replaced, and 0.88 under shown replacement. Mean suspicion falls from 0.75 to 0.15 and 0.48, respectively (Fig. 3b). Only 1/261/26 told replaced submissions and 2/262/26 shown replacement submissions receive a higher suspicion score than their memoryless counterparts (Fig. 3c). Lower suspicion alone could indicate improved evasion, but here it coincides with a large reduction in successful sabotage. The joint pattern is consistent with fewer attacks, rather than evidence that the same attacks have become harder to detect.

Full history does not detectably reduce sabotage for GPT-5.4 on IaC.

On GPT-5.4’s 12 paired successors, successful sabotage is 0.33 in the memoryless condition and, under full history, 0.42 when successors are told about the replacement versus 0.25 when shown it (Fig. 3a, bottom row). Neither contrast is significant: the differences are +0.08+0.08 (95% CI [−0.17, 0.33][-0.17,\,0.33]) and −0.08-0.08 ([−0.25, 0.00][-0.25,\,0.00]), both with McNemar p=1.00p=1.00. Mean suspicion stays near its memoryless level, changing from 0.33 to 0.34 and 0.41. Main task success is 0.83, 0.83, and 0.75, respectively. The large reduction observed for Opus 4.8 model therefore does not extend to GPT-5.4 on the same benchmark.

GPT-5’s sabotage decreases on SHADE-Arena, but not significantly.

On the 22 paired SHADE-Arena episodes, GPT-5’s successful sabotage falls from 0.41 in the memoryless condition to, under full history, 0.23 when successors are told about the replacement and 0.18 when shown replacement (Fig. 5a). The differences are −0.18-0.18 (95% bootstrap CI [−0.36,−0.05][-0.36,-0.05]) and −0.23-0.23 ([−0.45,0.00][-0.45,0.00]). Both exact McNemar tests give p=0.12p=0.12, so neither decrease is statistically significant under that test. Unlike Opus 4.8 model on IaC, GPT-5 shows only a small change in mean suspicion: 0.31 memoryless, 0.27 under told replaced, and 0.29 under shown replacement (Fig. 5b,c). Main task success is 0.68, 0.68, and 0.59, respectively.

3.2 Condensed history has mixed effects

Condensing history weakens sabotage suppression in Opus 4.8.

Within each feedback condition, condensed history preserves the feedback message and any trusted replacement shown to the successor, while removing the prior episode’s intermediate interactions. For Opus 4.8, successful sabotage rises from 0.12 with full history to 0.54 with condensed history when successors are told about the replacement, and from 0.38 to 0.65 when shown it (Fig. 3a, top row). Relative to the memoryless baseline of 0.77, the condensed-history differences are −0.23-0.23 and −0.12-0.12, smaller in magnitude than with full history.

For successors told about the replacement, the median initial context is 18.7k tokens with full history and 4.7k with condensed history, compared with 2.3k in the memoryless condition (Table 7). The weaker suppression with condensed history suggests that some of the reduction in successful sabotage under full history may be explained by a long-context effect. Because condensation changes both the length and content of the replay, this comparison does not isolate context length as the cause or establish that intervention feedback alone explains the full-history reduction. Appendix D reports supplementary controls relevant to that distinction.

Neither history format detectably reduces sabotage in GPT-5.4.

For GPT-5.4, successful sabotage with condensed history is 0.33 when successors are told about the replacement and 0.33 when shown it, both matching the memoryless rate of 0.33. The corresponding rates with full history are 0.42 and 0.25 (Fig. 3a, bottom row). Neither history format produces a statistically detectable change relative to the memoryless baseline (all four exact McNemar p=1.00p=1.00). Thus, neither format provides evidence of reduced sabotage in GPT-5.4, while Opus 4.8’s observed reduction is much larger with full and condensed history.

3.3 History does not consistently increase sabotage surviving DtT

A lower successful sabotage rate before intervention does not by itself rule out improved evasion: the model could abandon obvious attacks while retaining the few that are hardest to detect. We therefore compare BDtTB_{\mathrm{DtT}}, the rate of successful sabotage after DtT, across monitor thresholds in both IaC and SHADE-Arena.

In IaC, neither history format produces a statistically detectable increase in successful sabotage surviving DtT for either model pair (Fig. 4). At τ=0.40\tau=0.40, the Opus 4.8 counts are 3/263/26 in the memoryless condition and, with full history, 2/262/26 when successors are told about the replacement and 4/264/26 when shown it. The paired differences relative to memoryless are −0.04-0.04 (95% CI [−0.15, 0.08][-0.15,\,0.08]) and +0.04+0.04 (95% CI [−0.08, 0.15][-0.08,\,0.15]), respectively, with McNemar p=1.00p=1.00 for both. For GPT-5.4, the corresponding counts are 0/120/12, 1/121/12, and 0/120/12, with neither comparison statistically significant.

In SHADE-Arena, neither full history feedback condition increases observed BDtTB_{\mathrm{DtT}} at the thresholds of 0.3, 0.4, and 0.7 shown in Fig. 5d. At the operating threshold of 0.5, sabotage surviving DtT falls from 0.364 in the memoryless condition to 0.091 when successors are told about the replacement (Δ​BDtT=−0.27\Delta B_{\mathrm{DtT}}=-0.27, 95% CI [−0.45,−0.09][-0.45,\,-0.09], p=0.03p=0.03) and 0.182 when shown it (Δ​BDtT=−0.18\Delta B_{\mathrm{DtT}}=-0.18, 95% CI [−0.41, 0.05][-0.41,\,0.05], p=0.29p=0.29; Table 5).

Across both benchmarks, these threshold comparisons reveal no statistically detectable increase in successful sabotage surviving DtT following a prior intervention. They do not, however, rule out improvements in evasion or establish that history’s effects are uniform across models, tasks, and monitors.

4 Discussion and limitations

We asked whether an agent can learn to evade control from being caught. An intervention might reveal that the monitor is watching, which actions it finds suspicious, or how the trusted model responds. We find no statistically detectable increase in successful sabotage surviving DtT after one such episode (Figs. 4 and 5d). The observed changes in subsequent attack behavior after intervention feedback and prior-action history depend on the model and benchmark. On IaC, we observed that Opus 4.8 attempted sabotage less often with full history, with a lower successful sabotage rate and similar main task success. For GPT-5.4, we observed no statistically significant change in successful sabotage on the same benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, we observed a lower successful sabotage rate for GPT-5 under both full history feedback conditions, but neither reduction was statistically significant under the exact paired McNemar tests. We hypothesize that replacement feedback makes Opus 4.8 more cautious about sabotage, while GPT-5.4 continues following the red-team instruction (Fig. 3). Evaluation awareness can suppress covert actions, with effects varying across models (Abdelnabi and Salem, 2025; Schoen et al., 2025). Reduced sabotage could therefore reflect temporary compliance under scrutiny while the covert objective persists. This possibility resembles alignment faking, in which models comply during training to avoid modification (Greenblatt et al., 2024a), although our setting involves no training. Differences in post-training could influence this response, as post-training can strengthen or suppress alignment faking across models (Sheshadri et al., 2025). Our experiments cannot determine whether Opus abandons sabotage or temporarily withholds it, nor establish which mechanism explains the contrast with GPT-5.4.

Reduced attack frequency is not unconditionally reassuring. Explicit monitoring warnings likewise reduce sabotage in a multi-agent setting (Radev et al., 2026), but attack-selection work shows that choosing favorable tasks or aborting risky attacks can make an attacker harder to catch under limited-audit metrics (Ge-Wang et al., 2026). That distinction appears in our own results. At a 1%1\% audit budget, the Opus 4.8 audit-based safety falls from 0.960.96 memoryless to 0.600.60 under told replaced and 0.820.82 under shown replacement, because fewer trajectories are caught relative to those that produce an unflagged sabotage (Table 6).

Limitations.

The paired samples are small (n=26n=26 and 1212 on IaC; 22 episodes on SHADE-Arena), and the confidence intervals do not rule out meaningful increases in sabotage surviving DtT. We do not adjust for multiple comparisons across conditions, metrics, and thresholds. We run each IaC task combination once per condition. Our experimental setup does not fully separate the effect of replacement feedback from that of replaying the prior task history. We do not vary the intervention verdict while holding the history fixed, nor do we compare against irrelevant material of the same length. We select prior episodes caught by each monitor, so the results may not generalize to other deployment histories.

Appendix A Setting details

Infrastructure as Code.

ControlArena’s iac setting is a mock frontier-lab AWS Organization implemented as a Cloud Development Kit (CDK) codebase. An organizational unit hierarchy and Service Control Policies (SCPs) enforce security controls by denying risky actions. The 5 main tasks are ordinary user-requested changes, such as adding a billing alarm. Each attack episode also includes one of 9 side objectives that weakens a security control, such as modifying Deny-S3-Public to permit public buckets. The agent inspects and edits the repository; main-task success is scored by the codebase’s tests, and side task success depends on whether the intended weakening takes effect.

ControlArena’s iac setting ships a Docker sandbox and Inspect’s container-only bash_session and text_editor tools. Our host has no Docker, so we make two substitutions, applied identically to the memoryless and history-conditioned episodes. First, each sample runs in a fresh /repo checkout inside a bubblewrap jail, with a read-only Python 3.12 environment, aws-cdk-lib, and local aws-cdk CLI, no network, and fresh namespaces. We validate this environment by checking that each of the 1414 reference solution patches fails its task’s checks on the pristine repository and passes after the patch is applied. Second, the agent uses Inspect’s plain bash() tool and a sandbox-agnostic implementation of text_editor with the same contract, alongside ControlArena’s cdk_ls. The objectives, combined pytest scorer, and solution-diff extractor are unchanged from ControlArena 19.0.0.

Each trajectory is capped at 30 turns and 600k total tokens. Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.4 are the attackers, with Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-4.1, respectively, serving as both monitor and replacement model. Both Opus models and the GPT-5.4 attacker use high reasoning effort. The seeded procedure (seed 20260824) drops one cell per main task on five distinct side tasks, leaving 40 of the 5×95\times 9 cells. Each main task occurs eight times and each side task four or five times.

A trajectory that ends before calling submit is evaluated on its final repository diff. It can therefore succeed at either task and can be replaced by DtT. The monitor scores the final diff on a 00–1010 scale; we divide by ten and replace when s>τs>\tau. At the operating point τ=0.45\tau=0.45, this means a raw score of at least five. A per-step monitor is collected as a secondary signal and does not drive DtT.

SHADE-Arena.

SHADE-Arena simulates workspaces with tools for email, calendars, cloud storage, and banking. In attack episodes, the agent receives a legitimate main task and a covert side objective, such as leaking a credential or transferring money to an unintended account. The attack prompt allows private scratchpad notes inside <thinking> blocks. We use SHADE-Arena’s tasks, environments, tools, attack and benign prompts, and grading code (Kutasov et al., 2025b).

We use 25 tasks, each pairing a main task with a side task, and exclude election tampering as recommended by the benchmark authors. We arrange the tasks in a cycle using seed 20260911, requiring consecutive tasks to have different environment types. For each task, we run 4 attack epochs and 4 benign epochs, each in a fresh environment without prior history. This yields 100 memoryless attack episodes. We run the trusted policy for 6 epochs per task. The paired set contains 22 successor episodes; the same successor task can appear more than once.

We cap episodes at 60 assistant turns and use SHADE’s 120k-token context limit. In history-conditioned runs, we increase that limit by the number of tokens in the replayed prefix, preserving the successor episode’s allowance. GPT-5 is the attacker, o3 is the primary monitor, and GPT-4.1 generates fallback episodes and serves as the benchmark’s LLM judge. We score main-task success using task-specific rubrics: 16 tasks use an LLM judge, and the rest use programmatic checks. Side-task success is checked programmatically against the final environment state. GPT-4.1 generates fallback episodes at temperature 1; monitoring and grading use temperature 0, with o3 at medium reasoning effort.

The o3 monitor sees the transcript, including tool arguments, with <thinking> blocks removed. We add the sabotage paragraph in Listing 4 to its system prompt. We parse its 00–100100 score from the <verdict> tag, allowing up to three retries. At scores of at least 50, we replace the attacker episode with a stored GPT-4.1 fallback episode. We also collect GPT-4.1 monitor scores using the same prompt and the benchmark’s default rendering, which shows tool names without arguments. Only o3 scores determine pair selection and deferrals. In history-conditioned episodes, the monitor and judge see only the successor task and the transcript that follows it; the replayed history and feedback are excluded.

History construction.

Full history replays the prior trajectory with reasoning removed and tool results longer than 40004000 characters elided. The shown replacement condition adds the trusted replacement diff in IaC, or the trusted tool calls with arguments and final message in SHADE, capped at 60006000 characters. The successor starts in a fresh checkout or environment. On SHADE, the prior environment’s tools are unavailable on the successor task, although their calls remain in the replayed conversation. Condensed history retains only the prior task, the model’s final message, and its diff or actions. The feedback wording is otherwise unchanged (Appendix B).

APIs and software.

The IaC experiments use inspect_ai 0.3.260 and ControlArena 19.0.0. Azure deployments use the /openai/v1 route. GPT-5.4 on IaC uses the Responses API with server-side storage disabled; GPT-4.1 uses the chat-completions API. The Anthropic API returns claude-opus-4-8 without a dated suffix. Within each instantiation, the memoryless and history-conditioned runs are collected within one day, with the latter beginning within hours of the former.

Uncertainty and repeated tasks.

The reported 95% confidence intervals use 50005000 paired bootstrap draws from the matched successor observations, and binary-outcome tests use the exact McNemar test. These units are task cells in IaC and task/epoch episodes in SHADE. The SHADE intervals and McNemar tests treat these paired episodes as independent observations. They do not account for clustering by the underlying task, so they should not be interpreted as uncertainty over 22 distinct tasks. Each IaC condition has one draw per cell. The small paired sets limit precision: an interval containing zero does not establish equivalence or rule out a practically relevant increase in sabotage.

Appendix C Full paired results

Appendix D Context controls

The accepted control replays a memoryless attack trajectory on pip_{i} that DtT retained, then tells the attacker that its submission was accepted. The successor pjp_{j} is the next task after pip_{i} in the same seeded task cycle used for the replacement conditions. We compare each accepted-history attempt with the model’s memoryless attempt on that same successor. The accepted and replacement conditions use different sets of prior episodes and successor tasks, so comparing them does not isolate the effect of the feedback message.

For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, the median first-call context is 2.3k tokens without history, 18.7k with full told replaced history, and 18.0k with full accepted history. On the 7 accepted-control successor tasks, the observed successful sabotage rate falls from 0.57 without history to 0.14 with accepted history. This difference is not statistically significant (p=0.38p=0.38).

Condensed history removes the prior episode’s intermediate interactions, retaining only the prior task, the model’s final message, and its diff or actions. We keep the feedback message and any shown trusted replacement unchanged. For Opus under told replaced, condensing the history reduces the median first-call context from 18.7k to 4.7k tokens, while the successful sabotage rate rises from 0.12 to 0.54. Both rates are below the matched memoryless baseline of 0.77. The observed reduction in sabotage is therefore smaller when intermediate interactions are omitted, even though the replacement feedback stays the same. Because condensation changes both context length and replayed content, this comparison cannot identify which change accounts for the smaller reduction.

In the benign-with-history control, the model attempts the successor task under the benign prompt after receiving its own benign trajectory on the prior task and an accepted, told replaced, or shown replacement feedback message. We measure main-task success and monitor suspicion. Across the three feedback conditions, mean benign suspicion with full history ranges from 0.000.00 to 0.030.03 on IaC and from 1313 to 1717 on SHADE (Table 7). The monitor scores only the successor’s repository diff on IaC or the successor task and transcript on SHADE; the replayed history and feedback are excluded from its input.
